articles.title: Quantum Discovery Reveals Why More Powerful Lasers Can Actually Slow Atoms Down
articles.dek: Scientists have discovered that two carefully timed laser pulses can move atomic layers in a quantum material more effectively than a single, more powerful pulse.
paragraphs: Scientists have discovered that two carefully timed laser pulses can move atomic layers in a quantum material more effectively than a single, more powerful pulse. Published in Nature Physics , the research shows that increasing light intensity can actually limit atomic motion, while controlling when the energy arrives can overcome that restriction.

The discovery comes from researchers at the Universities of Würzburg and Rostock and ETH Zurich, who investigated tungsten ditelluride (WTe 2 ), a material known as a sliding ferroelectric. Its neighboring atomic layers can shift sideways against each other, much like two palms pressed together.

“What makes this particularly exciting is that the relative motion of the atomic layers can influence a range of material properties, such as ferroelectricity and topology,” explains Gerrit Horstmann, first author of the study and head of an Emmy Noether junior research group at the University of Würzburg.

Ultrashort laser pulses can change a crystal’s structure by transferring energy to its electrons. As the electrons respond, they exert forces on atomic nuclei, setting the atoms in motion. These processes occur within femtoseconds, with each femtosecond lasting just one millionth of a billionth of a second.

Increasing the laser’s intensity might seem like an obvious way to produce greater movement, but the researchers found that this approach has a fundamental limitation. “Under very strong excitation, electrons are promoted into high-energy states that counteract the directed motion of the atoms. The additional light energy then no longer produces a correspondingly larger displacement of the atomic layers; instead, it effectively slows them down,” explains Gerrit Horstmann.

To bypass this limitation, the team divided the laser energy between two weaker pulses delivered at different times. After the first pulse, the excited electrons have time to partially relax before the second pulse arrives. By adjusting the delay, the researchers can reinforce the sliding motion of the atomic layers, similar to pushing a child on a swing at precisely the right moment.

“Timing opens up an additional way to make optimal use of the interaction between electrons and atomic motion,” says Horstmann. Rather than forcing the atoms to move with increasingly powerful pulses, the technique uses the material’s own electronic and atomic dynamics to achieve more effective control. The approach follows a familiar principle: “Work smarter, not harder!”

Controlling how atomic layers slide could eventually provide a way to switch technologically useful properties, including ferroelectric polarization, with less energy. The technique may be particularly valuable for ultrathin materials such as WTe 2 , which can consist of only a few atomic layers and are being explored for compact electronic devices.

Although practical applications remain a longer-term goal, the findings establish a strategy for manipulating quantum materials through the timing of light pulses rather than simply increasing their intensity. As the researchers put it, “Work smarter, not harder!”

articles.title: Einstein Was Right Again: Scientists Discover Chemical Bonds That Defy Textbook Rules
articles.dek: Scientists have uncovered direct evidence that Einstein’s theory of relativity changes how atoms form triple chemical bonds in heavy elements.
paragraphs: Scientists have uncovered direct evidence that Einstein’s theory of relativity changes how atoms form triple chemical bonds in heavy elements.

A fundamental rule of chemical bonding begins to break down when atoms become sufficiently heavy. Chemists at Brown University have found direct experimental evidence that Einstein’s theory of relativity changes the structure of triple bonds, challenging a model that has been taught in chemistry classrooms for generations.

The discovery, published in Science , comes from experiments involving carbon and bismuth, a heavy element whose electrons are strongly influenced by relativistic effects. “This idea that relativity is important in heavy elements has been around since the 1970s,” said Lai-Sheng Wang, a Brown chemistry professor and the study’s corresponding author. “But we show direct spectroscopic evidence that what we learned in high school about chemical bonding isn’t true in heavy elements.”

Chemical bonds form when atoms share electrons, creating an attraction that holds their positively charged nuclei together. In the conventional description of a triple bond, three shared electron pairs produce one sigma bond and two pi bonds. The sigma bond forms through direct overlap along the axis connecting the nuclei, while the pi bonds involve electron density extending to either side of that axis.

This arrangement accurately describes many bonds involving lighter elements. In heavier atoms, however, the strong positive charge of the nucleus causes some electrons to move at speeds where relativistic effects become significant. These effects strengthen a phenomenon called spin-orbit coupling, which links an electron’s spin to its orbital motion and changes how electrons participate in bonding.
“The boundary between a sigma bond and a pi bond is now sort of smeared,” Wang said. “We still have three bonds, but we don’t really strictly have a sigma or a pi anymore.”

To investigate this effect, Brown doctoral students Deniz Kahraman and Jie Hui, working with Wang and their colleagues, produced molecules containing carbon and bismuth. They cooled the molecules to temperatures near absolute zero before examining them with photoelectron spectroscopy, a technique that uses light to eject electrons and measures their energies to determine how strongly they were bound.

The resulting spectra provided evidence of a triple bond unlike the conventional arrangement. Instead of one sigma bond and two pi bonds, the carbon-bismuth bond exhibited characteristics consistent with one pi bond and two hybrid sigma-pi bonds. This experimentally observed structure supports theoretical predictions that relativistic spin-orbit coupling can fundamentally alter bonding in heavy elements.

The findings could influence how chemists describe bonds involving heavy elements, particularly as researchers explore their potential in advanced technologies. Bismuth has attracted attention as a possible alternative to toxic lead in next-generation solar cells. It is also being investigated in quantum materials and research relevant to quantum computing.

Understanding how relativistic effects influence its chemical bonds may help scientists develop more accurate descriptions of bismuth-containing compounds and other heavy-element materials. The new evidence could eventually change how these bonds are presented in chemistry textbooks.
“Maybe this will become the new textbook idea as we are dealing with more and more heavy chemistry of the heavy elements,” Wang said.
The work was funded by the U. S. National Science Foundation (CHE-2403841) and the U. S. Department of Energy (DE-SC0008501).

articles.title: JWST tracks more than 100 magnified stellar events in the Dragon galaxy
articles.dek: Using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), a team of astronomers identified 104 magnified stellar events in a galaxy known as the Dragon, located around 6. 5 billion…
paragraphs: Using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), a team of astronomers identified 104 magnified stellar events in a galaxy known as the Dragon, located around 6. 5 billion light-years away. This discovery more than doubles the previous record of 44 such detections in the same galaxy. Because these kinds of events reveal some of the most luminous stars and likely the presence of dark matter, this study offers a rare look at the galaxy's stellar population along with a possible hint at the nature of dark matter.
The paper, describing the record-breaking discovery, was published in Astronomy & Astrophysics on Sept. 30.

The light from the Dragon galaxy, at redshift 0. 725, is stretched and magnified by a massive galaxy cluster called Abell 370. A portion of the galaxy is stretched into an arc, famously called the Dragon arc. This phenomenon is called gravitational lensing. But the lensing effect is not the same everywhere. Along certain lines called caustics, the light from the Dragon can get focused so strongly that the light's brightness can increase dramatically. This is because a galaxy cluster is not a uniform blob and its gravity bends light by different amounts in different places.

The cluster's own stars, and possibly dark matter, create small distortions too. They can break a single caustic line into "microcaustics." As the background galaxy moves slowly relative to the lensing cluster, individual stars in it drift across these microcaustics, creating a caustic crossing event.

At the crossing, two of the star's images merge and the star reaches maximum brightness, up to hundreds or thousands of times its normal level. Once it is done crossing, those two images vanish, and the star fades back within days to weeks. Because the events are temporary, astronomers find them by comparing images of the same distorted region or arc taken at different times.
In this new study, led by José María Palencia of the Institute of Physics of Cantabria, researchers compared JWST images collected from 2022 to 2024 to look for changes in brightness.

Since the images were taken at slightly different angles, the team made corrections to prevent any false residues or leftovers when subtracting images to find the brightness changes. They also removed bright unrelated objects, the galaxy's bright core and other contaminants that could be mistaken for flares. Then, they measured the normal noise level using another image of the same galaxy that lies far from the critical curve, the line where magnification is strongest, and therefore has no microlensing.

After merging repeated detections across filters and observations, the team detected 104 unique stellar events. "... we obtain a catalog of 104 unique CCEs in the Dragon arc, which currently represents the largest sample of highly magnified star candidates identified in a single galaxy," the team writes in the paper.

Only the most luminous stars can be detected through these events, which means the stars astronomers catch are almost always supergiants. They come in two main types: blue supergiants (BSGs) and red supergiants (RSGs). Blue ones are hot and shine mostly at short wavelengths, while red supergiants are cool and emit mostly in the near-infrared. The ratio between the two types reveals the nature of the stellar population in the galaxy. Younger and more metal-poor populations produce more luminous blue supergiants, while higher metallicity and older populations evolve toward the red category.
A key question for the Dragon arc is what the blue-to-red ratio looks like and whether it points to a young, star-forming system or an older one.

The team carried out a color analysis, which showed roughly equal numbers of blue and red supergiants, giving a ratio of 1. "This suggests that both BSGs and RSGs contribute to the observed CCEs, in agreement with expectations for a relatively evolved, still star-forming system," the team says.

articles.title: How space weather powers auroras in the sky and threatens power grids on the ground
articles.dek: An aurora is one of nature's most spectacular light shows: It looks like green or red curtains rippling across the night sky.
paragraphs: An aurora is one of nature's most spectacular light shows: It looks like green or red curtains rippling across the night sky. When viewed from the ground, this colorful display might seem far away and disconnected from anything happening on Earth's surface.

But while these beautiful displays are part of a much larger process known as "space weather"—changes in Earth's space environment caused by activity from the sun—they're closely connected to electric currents that can flow through the ground under your feet.

Space weather can create a spectacle in the sky, while also driving electric currents that can damage power grids and other technological systems on the ground. Space physicists like us want to understand how space weather can affect infrastructure on Earth.

Our research shows that a single space weather event called a substorm , during which energy is released tens of thousands of miles away from Earth, can affect the ground within minutes. The strength of the impact can vary from place to place depending on the latitude and the structure of the soil and rock below your feet. The findings are published in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Space Physics .
Earth is constantly immersed in the solar wind: a stream of charged particles flowing outward from the sun. Occasionally, the sun releases a much larger eruption called a coronal mass ejection .

This cloud of charged particles and magnetic fields does not simply "hit" Earth and immediately cause power-grid failures. Instead, it can set off a chain of processes in space that can pose a threat to power grids.

First, when the coronal mass ejection reaches Earth, the charged particles and magnetic fields it carries interact with Earth's magnetosphere . The magnetosphere is the region of space around Earth dominated by its magnetic field.

If the coronal mass ejection's magnetic field is oriented in a certain way, it can connect with Earth's magnetic field on the side facing the sun. The solar wind then carries these connected field lines around Earth away from the sun and stretches them far out into space behind Earth. This process forms a long region of stretched magnetic field lines called the magnetotail.

Magnetic energy builds up in the magnetotail as the solar wind continues to push the field lines farther into space—until they come close enough to reconnect . Then, the stored energy is released in an explosive process known as a substorm . This release occurs on the side of Earth facing away from the sun, roughly 28,000 to 40,000 miles (45,000 to 65,000 kilometers) from Earth.

During the substorm, energetic particles shoot along the magnetic field lines toward Earth. When these particles collide with oxygen and nitrogen atoms in the upper atmosphere, about 56 to 93 miles (90 to 150 kilometers) overhead, they produce the glowing aurora.
These energetic particles also drive strong electrical currents in Earth's upper atmosphere . Rapid changes in these currents can cause Earth's magnetic field at the ground level to change sharply.
These changing magnetic fields can induce electric currents in the ground and in power lines, potentially damaging transformers and tripping circuit breakers.

articles.title: Scientists Discover a Hidden Eye Disease That Can Steal Your Night Vision
articles.dek: Researchers can spot signs of a newly identified genetic eye disease before light-sensing cells are lost by measuring how vision recovers in darkness.
paragraphs: Researchers can spot signs of a newly identified genetic eye disease before light-sensing cells are lost by measuring how vision recovers in darkness.

People with a newly identified genetic eye condition can see well for most of their lives before gradually losing peripheral vision and struggling to see at dusk or at night. The condition is linked to a gene already associated with a different eye disease, one that affects central vision first.

The two conditions arise from different variants, or versions, of the EFEMP1 gene. The newly identified variant, p. Arg140Trp, causes abnormally thick material to build up between cells in the eye. Researchers are calling the condition EFEMP1 -associated late-onset retinal degeneration, or L-ORD, although it has not been formally named.

L-ORD begins slowly at the periphery of the retina, the tissue at the back of the eye that converts light into signals the brain interprets as sight. Its gradual progression makes it difficult to detect. One useful clue is unusually slow recovery of vision when a person moves from a lighted setting into low light. This adjustment involves rod photoreceptors, the retinal cells specialized for seeing in dim conditions.

“We can detect a major abnormality in the way rod photoreceptors recover in darkness with retinas that still look structurally intact,” said Artur V. Cideciyan, PhD, an ophthalmology researcher and co-director of the Center for Hereditary Retinal Degenerations. “This gives us a functional marker of disease at a stage when photoreceptor cells have not yet been lost.”
The investigation began with a clinical description of a family in the United States in 1998.

“The different disease expression in this family was thought to be similar to a condition caused by C1QTNF5 gene variants. However, none of the variants associated with that disease were found,” Cideciyan said. “Our collaborators then discovered a new variant in the EFEMP1 gene that normally causes a different disease where the macula, which is tied to central vision, is affected first.”

The genetic finding allowed researchers to expand the investigation to multiple European families. They studied three unrelated families in different countries that shared the p. Arg140Trp variant and compared them with a separate family carrying p. Arg345Trp, the EFEMP1 variant responsible for the already-known condition affecting central vision.

Published in JAMA Ophthalmology , the research involved an international team that included scientists from the Scheie Eye Institute of the Perelman School of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania. Researchers from the University of Edinburgh, the University of Basel, Charles University, and the University of Bonn also contributed.

The researchers do not yet know how widespread p. Arg140Trp is or how many people have this form of L-ORD. They suspect it may be relatively rare, but larger studies are needed to establish its prevalence.

“Aging is a risk factor for many medical conditions, including retinal diseases such as age-related macular degeneration, the most common retinal condition of aging,” said Tomas S. Aleman, MD, a professor of ophthalmology and the other co-director of the Center for Hereditary Retinal Degenerations. “Lessons learned from these infrequent, late-onset genetic eye diseases offer glimpses at possible mechanisms of disease for much more frequent retinal problems.”

This study was supported by grants from the University of Edinburgh Chancellor’s Fellowship award, RS Macdonald Charitable Trust Seedcorn Award, the BrightFocus Foundation (M2024009N), the German Research Foundation (532367710), the Medical Research Council (MC_UU_00035/9, MC_UU_00007/10), the Swiss National Science Foundation (204285), the Ministry of Health of the Czech Republic (NW24-06-00083), Charles University in Prague (UNCE/24/MED/022 and SVV 2600631), and the Samuel G. Jacobson, MD, PhD, Memorial Fund.

articles.title: 100 buses long: Scientists map one of the world's largest known coral colonies
articles.dek: A huge coral colony stretching more than 1. 5 kilometers (0. 93 miles) along the outer reef of the Cocos (Keeling) Islands has been identified by researchers, making it one…
paragraphs: A huge coral colony stretching more than 1. 5 kilometers (0. 93 miles) along the outer reef of the Cocos (Keeling) Islands has been identified by researchers, making it one of the largest known coral colonies ever recorded.

The remarkable rose coral (Pachyseris) colony extends 1. 56 kilometers (0. 97 miles) in length—the equivalent of approximately 100 buses parked end to end—and occupies the outer reef slope between depths of 14 and 65 meters (46 and 213 feet).

Local dive operator Dieter Gerhard first spotted extensive areas of the coral more than 30 years ago, but it wasn't until researchers began mapping the reef that they realized just how extensive the formation was and that the sections may be connected as one enormous colony.

Working with researchers from the Queensland Museum and James Cook University, lead researcher Dr. JP Hobbs from Adelaide University spent months mapping the coral, using GPS to mark his progress between dives when he ran out of air before reaching its end. It took 12 dives to finally map the full extent of the colony.

The coral measures an average width of 36. 5 meters (120 feet) (covering an area of 56,940 m² (613,000 square feet), or more than three MCG playing areas), with additional sections extending a further 200 to 300 meters (656 to 984 feet) beyond the main colony.
But there's another fascinating mystery to solve: is this one giant coral organism, or multiple colonies that have fused together over time? Researchers are now using genetic testing to investigate.
Queensland Museum scientists are among the research team, with the discovery providing new insights into the unique coral communities of Australia's remote marine environments.

articles.title: A New Fiber Supplement Could Be a Game Changer for Millions With IBS
articles.dek: For people with IBS, a specially designed fiber blend could support a healthier gut without added pain or bloating, a trial alongside a low-FODMAP diet suggests.
paragraphs: For people with IBS, a specially designed fiber blend could support a healthier gut without added pain or bloating, a trial alongside a low-FODMAP diet suggests.

Cutting out foods that leave you bloated or in pain can bring welcome relief. For millions of people with irritable bowel syndrome, or IBS, however, a diet that eases discomfort can come with a trade-off. Restricting certain foods can also reduce fiber intake and the beneficial bacteria that help support gut health.

Researchers at Edith Cowan University (ECU) in Australia have tested a specially formulated fiber blend that could help address that dilemma. Called ur gut, the supplement combines high-amylose maize resistant starch with psyllium husk powder. In a small clinical trial, the blend changed the composition of participants’ gut bacteria without worsening their abdominal pain, bloating, diarrhea, or constipation.

IBS is common worldwide and affects nearly 11 percent of Australians. Its cause remains unknown, although stress, infection, and medication are potential triggers. Certain foods, poor sleep, psychological stress, hormonal fluctuations, and lifestyle factors can aggravate symptoms.
One common recommendation is a low-FODMAP diet, which limits certain carbohydrates that gut bacteria readily ferment.

“For years we’ve known that a diet low in fermentable oligosaccharides, disaccharides, monosaccharides, and polyols (FODMAPs) can relieve symptoms, but they can also reduce beneficial gut bacteria and negatively impact fiber intake over time,” said lead author Dr. Tina Yan.
“We wanted to find a way to build better gut health while following a low-FODMAP diet.”

Scientists at ECU’s Nutrition and Health Innovation Research Institute (NHIRI) developed the blend and trialed it in people with IBS who were following a low-FODMAP diet. Adding fiber in this setting requires care because bacteria can produce gas as they break it down.
“Traditionally, fermentable fibers can be difficult for people with IBS because they can increase gas production and discomfort,” Dr. Yan said.
“What’s exciting about this study is that participants maintained stable symptoms while showing meaningful improvements in their gut microbiota as well as in their gut-related anxiety.”
The changes in participants’ gut bacterial composition were significant, and their extent stood out to ur gut® co-creator Professor Amanda Devine.
“Changes of this magnitude are rarely seen with such a short intervention,” she said.

“The study demonstrated that our targeted dietary fiber blend positively reshaped the gut microbiome in people with IBS following a low-FODMAP diet, supporting beneficial bacteria linked to gut and mental health. This was great to see.”

The researchers suspect the explanation lies in how the blend’s two ingredients, resistant starch and psyllium husk, work together. Resistant starch escapes digestion in the small intestine, leaving it available for bacteria to ferment in the colon. Psyllium appears to slow that fermentation, allowing the starch to travel farther into the colon before bacteria break it down. The researchers believe this enhances the production of beneficial metabolites, substances the bacteria produce as they process the starch.

articles.title: New species of ground-dwelling bird, the largest of its kind, identified in same cave as Homo floresiensis
articles.dek: In 2009, researchers working in the Liang Bua cave on Flores Island came across a leg bone. The 190,000–120,000-year-old fossil was identified as a bird bone and set aside.
paragraphs: In 2009, researchers working in the Liang Bua cave on Flores Island came across a leg bone. The 190,000–120,000-year-old fossil was identified as a bird bone and set aside. Like many bird bones before it, it was overlooked and left to collect dust.

Now, about 17 years later, researchers have identified the fossil as belonging to a new extinct megapode species, a ground-dwelling, chicken-like bird. It's the first megapode fossil ever found in Wallacea and one of the largest of its kind, according to the study published in Alcheringa: An Australasian Journal of Palaeontology .

"It is one of the oldest bird remains we have found at Liang Bua …," Hanneke Meijer, a professor and curator of osteology at the University Museum of Bergen, said. "This is a period for which we have almost no data on birds, … so it is exciting that we can pinpoint this species to this period."

Megapodes split from other fowl-like birds during the Late Cretaceous, with researchers suggesting the group first emerged in Australasia before spreading their wings across eastern Indonesia, Melanesia, the Philippines and Australia, where they are found today, the study authors wrote.
According to Meijer, "Rather than sit on their nests, they (megapodes) lay their eggs in large mounds or burrows and then leave them there (and never look back)."
Despite megapodes' diverse and long history, the study reported that no bird fossil of one had ever been found in Wallacea.
Then researchers found this fossilized leg bone in one of Liang Bua's deepest layers. That's the same cave that held the ancient remains of Homo floresiensis, the study reported.

It sat unstudied for years until researchers began comparing it to living and extinct megapode species. They found it was unlike any other. Its toe joints differ in shape and position from those of other megapodes, and its leg shape and size suggest it was rather large.

All in all, the evidence suggested the fossil belonged to a new species. The researchers named it Megapodius rokusi, after Rokus Due Awe, the same individual who first recognized the bones of H. floresiensis and later identified the fossil as a bird bone.
"Due Awe was an incredible self-taught zooarchaeologist, and it is an honor to be able to name a species after him," Meijer said.

M. rokusi would have been rather large, weighing around 3. 9 kilograms (~8. 6 pounds), making it the largest Megapodius ever found. Today, it would even dwarf Flores Island's current megapode species, the orange-footed scrubfowl, which weighs only 0. 5–1. 2 kg (~1–3 pounds), the study reported.

Not much else can be said from a single fossil. Without wing bones, it is uncertain whether it could fly, and without other fossils, even its extinction is murky. The study reported that it may have vanished around the same time as Liang Bua's other extinct animals, including the giant stork, the dwarf Stegodon, H. floresiensis and vultures. Alternatively, it may have disappeared much earlier.

Even so, this bone fills a gap in the bird fossil record and, for Meijer, is a reminder of how much is still unknown. "Southeast Asia is considered a biodiversity hotspot, but it is important to realize that what we see today is only a remnant of what once was," Meijer said.
Meijer doubts this is the only megapode fossil in Wallacea. Because bird fossils have long been overlooked in favor of mammal bones, she expects more are out there, waiting to be discovered.

articles.title: Could a Nasal Spray Stop Alzheimer’s Before Memory Loss Begins?
articles.dek: Protecting memory from Alzheimer’s may one day involve a nasal spray, with encouraging results in animals and evidence that its particles also protect human neurons grown in…
paragraphs: Protecting memory from Alzheimer’s may one day involve a nasal spray, with encouraging results in animals and evidence that its particles also protect human neurons grown in the lab.

Alzheimer’s disease damages the connections that allow brain cells to communicate, threatening memory. A nasal spray containing tiny particles naturally released by cells has helped protect those connections in an animal model of the disease. The treatment both prevented memory deficits and countered cognitive decline after it had begun.

The particles, called extracellular vesicles, are small packages that cells release into their surroundings. Those used in this study came from cells of the amniotic membrane, the tissue lining the sac that surrounds a developing fetus. Researchers at the Università Cattolica del Sacro Cuore, Fondazione Policlinico Universitario A. Gemelli IRCCS, and the E. Menni Research Center of Fondazione Poliambulanza reported the findings in Translational Neurodegeneration .

When administered through the nose to animals that mimic features of Alzheimer’s disease, the vesicles reached the hippocampus, a brain region crucial for memory and particularly vulnerable to the disease. There, they entered both neurons and microglia, cells that monitor conditions in the brain and help defend it. The treatment counteracted neuroinflammation and protected neuronal function, particularly at synapses, the connections through which nerve cells transmit information. These effects were accompanied by a significant improvement in cognitive abilities.

The choice of amniotic membrane cells grew out of years of placental research by Professor Ornella Parolini, a full professor of applied biology and scientific director of IRCCS Ospedale “Casa Sollievo della sofferenza.” Her work has focused on these cells and the substances they release, collectively known as the secretome, investigating their protective and regenerative effects in various experimental models. The E. Menni Research Center, led by Parolini, contributed expertise in isolating and characterizing the cells and identifying the molecules they produce.

The research combined the expertise of Professor Claudio Grassi, whose team at the Università Cattolica studies brain inflammation and plasticity, with work by Professor Salvatore Fusco on the vesicles’ effects in the brain. Lead authors Dr. Andrea Papait and Dr. Francesca Natale helped connect these findings, investigating how amniotic extracellular vesicles influence brain inflammation, neuronal function, and memory.
The findings also suggest that effective Alzheimer’s treatments may need to address more than the buildup of harmful proteins in the brain.

Professor Fusco explains: “The study suggests the need to direct research into Alzheimer’s therapies by focusing not only on counteracting the accumulation of toxic compounds like beta-amyloid and tau, but also by paying close attention to the cellular environment in which neurons live (e. g. , microglia and astrocytes) and the molecular signals (e. g. , cytokines or microRNAs) exchanged by these cells, which can influence synapse function.”

To investigate the protective effects in human cells, researchers used skin biopsies collected from patients with Alzheimer’s disease and healthy individuals at the Policlinico’s Memory Clinic. From those samples, they generated pluripotent stem cells, which can develop into different cell types, and then used those cells to produce human neurons.
The vesicles also showed protective effects in these laboratory-grown neurons, extending the evidence to experimental human models and giving the study a closer connection to patients.
Professor Grassi emphasizes that the findings are encouraging but still preliminary.

“These are preclinical results that require further validation in humans and do not yet represent an available therapy for Alzheimer’s disease, but they point to a very promising direction: understanding whether some of the mechanisms through which the placenta naturally regulates inflammation and protects tissues could offer new tools for the treatment of neurodegenerative diseases and, more generally, whether the use of extracellular vesicles represents a new frontier for the treatment of neurological diseases.”

articles.title: Game theory helps SETI search for alien civilizations
articles.dek: The search for extraterrestrial intelligence (SETI) is mostly concerned with where to look for technosignatures from another civilization.
paragraphs: The search for extraterrestrial intelligence (SETI) is mostly concerned with where to look for technosignatures from another civilization. Between 2012 and 2015, SETI's Project Phoenix targeted about 1,000 sun-like stars for signs of intelligent life. But where to look might not be as important as when to look, according to scientists at SETI.

In a new paper, scientists outline the effort to search for signals not only in the right place, but at the right time. The paper is " A Technosignature Survey Of The Anti-Solar Point: The SETI Institute's Largest-Ever Campaign With The Allen Telescope Array ," and it was presented at the 77th International Astronautical Congress. The authors are Isabel Gerrard and Sofia Z. Sheikh. Gerrard is the technosignature researcher with Breakthrough Listen at the University of Oxford, and Sheikh is a SETI Institute research scientist.
The work is also published on the arXiv preprint server.

The new search effort doesn't do away with the "where" aspect of the search. Since life exists around stars, this search is still focused on stars, or rather the planets that orbit them. But it's different this time. This time it involves a point that changes over time, called the antisolar point. It's the point in space-time that's directly opposite the sun from the perspective of an observer.

Imagine a line extending from the sun, through an observer on Earth, and out the other side. It's not fixed in place; it's an abstract point defined by changing coordinates that shifts as the Earth orbits the sun.

This new SETI effort is also inspired by game theory. Game theory is a way of anticipating another player's moves in a game, when their moves are also based on their anticipations of your next move. The most well-known example of game theory is probably the prisoner's dilemma. In this case, the other player is another intelligent civilization conducting their own SETI-like effort.
What it boils down to is trying to predict when and where we can detect a purposeful transmission from another civilization and send our own, and also when and where they're doing the same.
"We borrow from game theory the concept of Schelling points to hypothesize spacetime coordinates where both we and an extraterrestrial agent might send and search for a signal," the authors write.

Schelling points are also called focal points in game theory. "From the perspective opposite the sun, an extraterrestrial agent could detect Earth transiting within the habitable zone. Thus, this anti-solar point (ASP) poses a shared and salient Schelling point."

Resources are limited, and the better we or an alien civilization can use them, the greater the chances of success. If they can figure out the most effective time and place to send a radio signal, they increase their chances of success. The same is true for us. There's a synergy in it.

"A Schelling point is a default solution two agents both naturally arrive at, without communication, because of some shared cultural understanding of prominence in the given context," the authors write. "The predictability of a Schelling point relies on a common understanding of the prominent features in this context, and the mutual awareness of each other's knowledge."

So without any prior communication, both we and another extraterrestrial agent would identify the same place to send and receive signals: the antisolar point. The choice is based on our shared understanding of astronomical transits, or what we call the transit method in the hunt for exoplanets. It's almost certain that another civilization would also use this method because it presents itself naturally.

"It follows that if an ETA (extraterrestrial agent) also used the transit method in their search for life, they would detect Earth against the sun as habitable and classify Earth as an eligible target for interstellar communication," the researchers explain.

At the midpoint of Earth's transit in front of the sun, from the ETA's perspective, Earth would be directly between them and the sun. "From the perspective opposite the sun, once each year an extraterrestrial agent could detect Earth transiting within the habitable zone, thus this antisolar point poses a shared and salient time-coordinate Schelling point," the authors write.

articles.title: NASA Announces $1 Million to Students for Moon Base Challenge
articles.dek: On Sunday, NASA announced the opening of its $1 million Moon Base Student Challenge during a MAX POWER event at Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex in Florida.
paragraphs: On Sunday, NASA announced the opening of its $1 million Moon Base Student Challenge during a MAX POWER event at Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex in Florida. As part of a Golden Age of Science, the competition invites student teams at U. S. high schools and post-secondary schools to contribute designs for the Moon Base.

“We’re looking for students ready to think creatively, work as a team, and take on real problems connected to NASA’s future on the Moon,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “You do not have to wait until graduation to contribute. Curiosity, creativity, and the willingness to tackle hard problems without obvious answers are exactly the qualities we need as we build what comes next.”

NASA is building a Moon Base where astronauts will live, work, and explore at the lunar South Pole region. A permanent human presence on the Moon paves the way for future crewed missions to Mars and requires talent from various industries and backgrounds.

“As we build and design the foundations of Moon Base, we want to leverage all the ingenuity and innovation to think of every consideration our explorers might need to live and work there,” said Carlos García-Galán, manager, Moon Base Program. “Students bring exactly the bold ideas that we’re looking for, and I’m looking forward to their fresh perspective. Ultimately, Moon Base is for them, people who will experience a world where humans are on the Moon to stay.”

The multiphase challenge supports NASA’s commitment to cultivating the technical skills of tomorrow’s aerospace workforce. For this challenge, student teams will design innovative solutions for Moon Base across six categories: power generation and storage, construction, life-support systems, surface mobility, communications networks, and astronaut safety. The challenge gives participants an opportunity to develop necessary skills for careers in the space industry while helping advance new concepts for Moon Base technologies.
Participants are required to register for the challenge through the NASA STEM Gateway. Registration is open until Jan. 25, 2027.

“Students are the next generation of explorers and innovators. Their unique perspectives are key to helping us envision a future away from Earth, and I’m excited to see the creativity and ingenuity spurred by this challenge,” said Elaine Ho, associate administrator for the Office of STEM Engagement at NASA Headquarters.

The Moon Base Student Challenge addresses authentic environmental and mission design parameters for life and operations on the lunar surface. The deliverables reflect industry skills – such as trade studies, concept proposals, and stakeholder briefings – allowing participants across technical, vocational, and various academic tracks to build career-relevant skills without requiring prior specialized engineering or technical experience.

The Office of STEM Engagement designed the challenge in collaboration with the Moon Base Program. The Institute of Competition Sciences administers the challenge through a contract with the NASA Center of Excellence for Collaborative Innovation within the agency’s Research and Technology Mission Directorate.

articles.title: 'Stupendously large' primordial black holes ruled out as a dark matter source
articles.dek: Primordial black holes are hypothetical objects that could have formed directly from dense clumps of matter in the very early universe.
paragraphs: Primordial black holes are hypothetical objects that could have formed directly from dense clumps of matter in the very early universe. If they exist, their dramatic origins would set them apart from the black holes we see today, which form when massive stars collapse. Some theories suggest that "stupendously large" primordial black holes could account for a significant share of the universe's elusive dark matter.

Yet new calculations by Nicholas Leister at the Mainz Institute for Theoretical Physics and colleagues show that even if these immense objects do exist, they can't make up any meaningful fraction of dark matter.
Their research has been published in Physical Review Letters .

Dark matter is thought to make up around 85% of the matter in the universe—but despite decades of intensive searching, physicists still don't know what it is really made from. One proposed candidate is a population of primordial black holes, each weighing at least 100 billion times as much as the sun. Named "stupendously large" black holes, these bodies would be even more massive than the largest supermassive black holes found at the centers of galaxies including the Milky Way.

In their study, Leister's team tested this possibility from a new angle. If primordial black holes were scattered randomly through space, some regions would contain more of them than others, purely by chance.

At first, each surplus of black holes would be balanced by a slight shortage of radiation. But as the universe expanded and its radiation thinned out, this balance would break down. The result would be patchy variations in the amount of dark matter relative to radiation.

After calculating the resulting strengths of these variations, the team compared their predictions with limits set by measurements of the cosmic microwave background (CMB). This subtle microwave signal is the faint afterglow of the Big Bang and can tell us how galaxies are spread across the largest scales of the universe. The fewer and heavier the black holes, the more uneven their random scattering becomes.
Through their analysis, Leister's team found that a substantial population of stupendously large primordial black holes would leave the balance between dark matter and radiation far too uneven.

This patchiness would imprint distinctive patterns on the CMB, but these patterns clearly aren't present in the signal. The result also challenges suggestions that primordial black holes helped seed the surprisingly massive early galaxies spotted by the James Webb Space Telescope.

The study doesn't rule out primordial black holes in this mass range altogether. Since the team assumed that all the black holes share the same mass, populations with a wide range of masses still need to be explored before their calculations can be fully conclusive. All the same, their results place tight new limits on how much these objects could contribute to dark matter.

With upcoming CMB experiments, including LiteBIRD and the Simons Observatory, the researchers predict that these limits would be tightened even further. They also hope to extend their analysis to even heavier black holes by searching for the gravitational waves that would have been released as they formed. Together, these efforts could ultimately help to narrow the search for the true identity of dark matter.

articles.title: NASA Space Telescope Meets Fiery End After Nearly 22 Years in Orbit
articles.dek: NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has returned to Earth after spending nearly 22 years in space, bringing an extraordinary mission of cosmic discovery to an end.
paragraphs: NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has returned to Earth after spending nearly 22 years in space, bringing an extraordinary mission of cosmic discovery to an end. The spacecraft reentered Earth’s atmosphere on Wednesday, more than two decades after launching in 2004.

Swift was a pioneering space observatory equipped with three telescopes capable of detecting different wavelengths of light. It was the first observatory of its kind, built to investigate some of the most powerful explosions in the universe.

The U. S. Space Force confirmed that Swift entered the atmosphere at 7:39 a. m. EST on November 4, above North Sumatra, Indonesia. The reported location was approximately 3. 4 degrees north latitude and 98. 6 degrees east longitude.
NASA anticipated that most of the spacecraft would burn up as it plunged through the atmosphere, although some pieces may have survived the descent.

When Swift launched in 2004, its primary goal was to study gamma-ray bursts, extraordinarily energetic explosions that rank among the most powerful events in the cosmos. The observatory was initially expected to operate for just two years, but it continued collecting valuable scientific data for more than two decades.

Over its remarkable lifetime, Swift became an exceptionally versatile tool for astronomers. Its instruments could observe several types of light, allowing researchers to investigate a wide range of cosmic phenomena. The spacecraft could also quickly turn toward sudden, short-lived bursts of energy and notify other observatories, giving scientists an opportunity to study events that might otherwise disappear before they could be examined.

These capabilities helped transform our understanding of the universe. Swift contributed to discoveries involving active galaxies powered by supermassive black holes, stars producing powerful X-ray flares, and the spectacular explosions of dying stars known as supernovas. Its observations also extended much closer to home, providing valuable information about comets and asteroids traveling through our own solar system.
What began as a two-year mission ultimately became nearly 22 years of exploring the universe, leaving behind a remarkable scientific legacy.

articles.title: NASA’s Perseverance Mars Rover Just Drove Farther Than Any Vehicle Beyond Earth
articles.dek: NASA’s self-driving Perseverance rover has broken the all-time off-world driving record and is now exploring ancient Martian terrain that could hold clues to the Red Planet’s…
paragraphs: NASA’s self-driving Perseverance rover has broken the all-time off-world driving record and is now exploring ancient Martian terrain that could hold clues to the Red Planet’s long-lost history.

NASA’s Perseverance rover has set a new record for driving on another world, traveling farther across the surface of Mars than any vehicle in history. On October 11, its total distance reached 28. 10 miles (45. 22 kilometers), surpassing the previous record of 28. 06 miles (45. 16 kilometers) held by NASA’s Opportunity rover, which operated on Mars from 2004 to 2018. Perseverance achieved the milestone on its 2,006th Martian day, known as a sol, completing in just five and a half years a journey that took Opportunity nearly 15.

The record was broken as Perseverance made its way toward a location called “Idubi,” passing through an area nicknamed “Lac de Charmes” just beyond the western edge of Jezero Crater. Scientists believe this region contains some of the most ancient terrain ever investigated in the solar system. Comparable rocks on Earth have largely disappeared because of erosion and plate tectonics (Mars doesn’t have tectonic plates). At Idubi, researchers hope to uncover evidence of ancient hydrothermal systems, where hot water once interacted with surrounding rock.

A major reason Perseverance has been able to travel so far is its sophisticated autonomous driving technology. Its navigation system, called AutoNav, allows the rover to analyze its surroundings and choose a safe route while moving. As it drives, Perseverance captures images, creates three-dimensional maps of potential obstacles, and determines how to travel between destinations chosen by engineers on Earth. NASA describes this ability as “thinking while driving.”

Unlike earlier rovers, Perseverance can perform these calculations while traveling at or close to its maximum speed. It has covered as much as 1,351 feet (412 meters) in a single Martian day. More than 90% of its total driving distance has involved AutoNav evaluating the terrain, a dramatic improvement over the roughly 5% achieved by the first Martian AutoNav system used by Opportunity and its twin rover, Spirit.

The difference in computing capability is equally remarkable. NASA’s first Mars rover, Sojourner, relied on just 20 measurement points to evaluate the ground ahead. Perseverance now analyzes 600,000 points every time it examines the terrain.

“It is an honor to be working on Perseverance at a moment when the technology has evolved to the point that drives like these are routine,” said Steven Lee, the project manager of the Curiosity and Perseverance rovers at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. “The original mission called for no more than 12. 4 miles of driving. We’ve blown well past that, and with all mobility systems fully operational and favorable extended-ground-life test results, we expect Perseverance to keep adding to this record for many years to come.”

NASA has already authorized the first extension of the Perseverance mission. The extended phase began in October and is expected to keep the rover investigating the rim of Jezero Crater through approximately the end of 2028.

Perseverance’s accomplishment builds on nearly three decades of robotic exploration on Mars. With each new generation, NASA has developed rovers capable of traveling greater distances and navigating increasingly challenging landscapes.

The journey began in 1997 with Sojourner, a small rover roughly the size of a microwave oven. During its 83-sol mission, it traveled approximately 330 feet (100 meters). In 2004, NASA sent the much larger, golf-cart-sized rovers Spirit and Opportunity to Mars. Although both were originally designed for missions lasting just 90 sols, they went on to far exceed expectations.

Spirit traveled 4. 8 miles (7. 7 kilometers) before its mission ended during the harsh Martian winter of 2010. Opportunity proved even more durable, operating for 5,111 sols and completing the first marathon-distance drive on another world in 2015. Its extraordinary journey established the distance record that Perseverance has now broken.
NASA’s Curiosity rover , which arrived at Gale Crater in 2012 and continues exploring Mars, has accumulated more than 23. 65 miles (38. 07 kilometers) of driving.
Perseverance is not simply traveling farther than its predecessors. Its ability to navigate independently has continued to improve since it landed on Mars.

articles.title: Want to fly to the moon? NASA is looking for new astronauts to help grow its Artemis program
articles.dek: Want to fly to the moon and help build a permanent lunar base ? NASA is accepting applications for a new astronaut class that will help grow the Artemis program.
paragraphs: Want to fly to the moon and help build a permanent lunar base ? NASA is accepting applications for a new astronaut class that will help grow the Artemis program.
Officials announced the news Saturday during a Kennedy Space Center air show promoting lunar exploration as well as advances in aviation and technology.
NASA's last call for new astronauts was two years ago. More than 8,000 applied, with 10 making the final cut in September 2025.

With only 32 active astronauts, the space agency needs more recruits as it looks to expand humanity's presence beyond low-Earth orbit as quickly as possible. April's lunar flyaround by the Artemis II crew kicked off the lunar campaign.
"We have far more work than we have astronauts," Artemis III commander Randy Bresnik told The Associated Press on Saturday.

Aspiring astronauts have between now and Dec. 3 to submit their applications. NASA expects to make its final selection by late 2027, with the new candidates beginning their training by early 2028—the same year that NASA intends to return astronauts to the lunar surface after an absence of more than half a century.
By then "we're going to have people on the moon—so don't delay," Bresnik urged potential candidates.

Bresnik and his three crewmates will blast into orbit next summer to practice docking their capsule with a pair of lunar landers, one built by Elon Musk's SpaceX and the other by Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin. Their mission will stick close to Earth—no lunar flyby—and serve as a dress rehearsal for the following year's Artemis IV mission that will attempt to land two astronauts near the lunar south pole.
The moon base will materialize as more rovers, robots, structures and power grids are launched.

Patience is essential for becoming an astronaut, noted Artemis III's Frank Rubio, whose 371 consecutive days in space is a U. S. endurance record. Candidates must also be U. S. citizens with college degrees and professional work experience.
The two years of mandatory training can be grueling, and it could take another several years on top of that before finally rocketing into space.

"It's important for them to realize most of that work is not going to the moon, right?" Rubio told the AP. "That will be about 1% of your experience. What you're doing is contributing to the mission of going to the moon."
This will be NASA's 25th astronaut class since the original Mercury Seven in 1959.

articles.title: NASA Awards Moon Base Transportation, Technology, Science Projects
articles.dek: NASA announced a suite of awards and mission updates on Saturday to expand the agency’s Moon Base exploration, science, and infrastructure capabilities.
paragraphs: NASA announced a suite of awards and mission updates on Saturday to expand the agency’s Moon Base exploration, science, and infrastructure capabilities. The investments will advance commercial robotic deliveries, a nuclear-powered rover named PROMISE, launch and orbital transfer services, and surface infrastructure as the agency works with American industry to establish a sustained presence on the Moon’s South Pole.
The agency shared the news at the MAX POWER aerospace expo and air show at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

“We are building the Moon Base mission by mission,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “Today’s announcements expand nearly every part of that campaign, using the playbook that carried NASA through its greatest eras: fly often, learn, apply those lessons, and get more better and more capable with every mission. When our astronauts return to the Moon, they will arrive with the first elements of the Moon Base already waiting for them on the surface.”

“In the eight months since Ignition, we’ve made incredible strides in accomplishing the near impossible: establishing a permanent outpost on the lunar surface,” said Carlos García-Galán, manager, Moon Base Program. “We’ve consolidated numerous efforts into a streamlined program, evolving our human exploration architecture into an iterative and sustained campaign for Moon Base technology development and implementation. Most importantly, we’ve taken action, awarding new contracts and forging new partnerships to accelerate development.”

To strengthen the cargo lander network needed to support the Moon Base, NASA selected eight companies for the next phase of its CLPS ( Commercial Lunar Payload Services ) initiative. The companies are eligible to compete for future lunar surface delivery missions under the new CLPS 2 contract:

Under the CLPS 2 framework, the companies will provide lunar delivery services, including managing, building, and operating landers that transport NASA science, technology, and infrastructure payloads to the Moon.

The CLPS 2 framework is a 10-year, multiple-award, indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity master contract with a combined maximum value of $10 billion. NASA increased the value of the current CLPS 1. 0 contract from $2. 6 billion to $4. 2 billion to support initial Phase One Moon Base objectives. The original CLPS contract will remain in place through November 2028, with an additional five-year period to complete awarded lunar deliveries through November 2033.

NASA also announced it is moving forward with development of PROMISE (Polar Rover for Observation, Mapping, and In-Situ Exploration) . Carrying science instruments and technology demonstrations, the six-wheeled rover will land at the Moon’s South Pole to characterize the surface and subsurface, assess resource potential, and provide data to enable landing site selection, as well as future infrastructure and exploration activities. The nuclear-powered rover can operate during long lunar nights and within permanently shadowed regions thought to harbor ice, which is crucial for a sustained human presence on the Moon.

The agency’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California, a division of Caltech, will manage the mission and build the rover from a combination of spare flight components and engineering test models for NASA’s Curiosity and Perseverance Mars rovers. Using proven hardware, software, and Mars rover operation approaches significantly reduces cost and enables integration and testing of the complex PROMISE rover on a shorter timeline. NASA has assessed the compatibility of the hardware with the lunar environment and determined it can tolerate the harsh conditions found near the Moon’s South Pole.

The PROMISE rover will carry a drill to extract regolith, or lunar dust, to characterize ice and other resources from approximately 3 feet (1 meter) below the surface, spectrometers for analyzing the chemical composition of surface material, temperature and radiation sensors, and visible-light cameras. It will demonstrate a next-generation, radiation-tolerant computing system, NASA’s High Performance Spaceflight Computing , and advanced autonomy sensors and algorithms. NASA is targeting late 2028 to launch PROMISE and planning an 18-month mission for the rover.

NASA awarded Blue Origin a $94 million base contract, with an option period worth an additional $140 million based on performance to deliver PROMISE to the lunar South Pole. The award expands the task order awarded in May 2026 to deliver two lunar terrain vehicles to the Moon. Blue Origin will use its Mark 1 lander to deliver and deploy the rover as part of the Moon Base’s first phase.

articles.title: NASA Seeks Next Generation of Explorers to Join Astronaut Corps
articles.dek: NASA is looking for the explorers who will help write the next chapter of human spaceflight.
paragraphs: NASA is looking for the explorers who will help write the next chapter of human spaceflight.

Applications are now open for the agency’s next class of astronauts, who will join NASA as America returns to the Moon, builds the Moon Base, and lays the groundwork for the first crewed missions to Mars.

The next generation of astronauts will train to operate on the lunar surface, live and work beyond Earth, and take on missions that will push the boundaries of human exploration farther than ever before.
U. S. citizens interested in joining the astronaut corps have until 11:59 p. m. EST Thursday, Dec. 3, to submit their completed application materials at:

“This is an extraordinary time to join NASA’s astronaut corps,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “The people we select could walk on the Moon, live and work at the Moon Base, and help pioneer the systems and operations that will ultimately carry crews to Mars. Those missions will demand technical excellence, sound judgment, teamwork, and courage. NASA’s astronaut corps has always called on remarkable Americans willing to take on extraordinary challenges in service to the nation. If you are ready to join that tradition, come help write the next chapter of humanity’s greatest adventure.”
NASA expects to make its final selection in late 2027 to begin training as the next class of astronaut candidates.
“The window is open. The mission is waiting. And the only thing missing from the greatest adventure humanity has ever embarked upon is you,” said NASA Deputy Administrator Matt Anderson.
The agency last opened applications in 2024. From more than 8,000 applications, 10 astronaut candidates were selected in 2025 and are currently completing nearly two years of training.

“For those who apply, becoming a NASA astronaut is more than a career opportunity,” said Scott Tingle, chief astronaut and chair of the Astronaut Selection Board at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston. “It is a chance to join a legacy of explorers who have pushed the boundaries of discovery and play a role in the missions that will shape humanity’s future in space. The next generation of astronaut candidates could help write history while inspiring future scientists, engineers, and explorers.”

Since the 1960s, NASA has selected 370 people to train as astronaut candidates for its increasingly challenging missions. The agency has 32 astronauts active in the astronaut corps, and selected applicants will join their ranks to study spacewalking, lunar geology, operations of high-performance aircraft, and more.

Those missions will demand technical excellence, sound judgment, teamwork, and courage. NASA’s astronaut corps has always called on remarkable Americans willing to take on extraordinary challenges in service to the nation. If you are ready to join that tradition, come help write the next chapter of humanity’s greatest adventure.”
NASA expects to make its final selection in late 2027 to begin training as the next class of astronaut candidates.
“The window is open. The mission is waiting. And the only thing missing from the greatest adventure humanity has ever embarked upon is you,” said NASA Deputy Administrator Matt Anderson.

The next generation of astronaut candidates could help write history while inspiring future scientists, engineers, and explorers.”

Since the 1960s, NASA has selected 370 people to train as astronaut candidates for its increasingly challenging missions.
